analysis.one_liner: Lets companies treat gig workers as independent contractors for tax purposes if a written contract test is met.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its introduction in March 2019, it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a detailed checklist into the tax code: if a company and a worker sign a written contract and the arrangement meets a list of factors, the worker counts as an independent contractor, not an employee, for federal tax purposes. Once that happens, the company owes no employer payroll taxes and no withholding obligations for that worker, and the IRS would be barred from reclassifying the worker retroactively if the company followed the rules. The bill trades that safe harbor for some new obligations on companies: they would have to withhold 5% of the first $20,000 paid under each contract and report payments to the IRS.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that rely on contractor labor — especially gig platforms like ride-share, delivery, and task apps — gain a clear, safe legal test and protection from IRS challenges to how they classify workers. Workers classified under the test get a modest benefit: 5% tax withholding on the first $20,000 of pay under a contract, which makes estimated taxes easier, and the right to ask the U.S. Tax Court to decide their employment status.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a bright-line safe harbor: if the written contract and the statutory factors are met, the provider is not treated as an employee and the payor is not treated as an employer for federal tax purposes.

It limits the IRS's ability to reclassify workers retroactively: if a company met the contract, reporting, and tax-payment requirements and showed a good-faith basis, a reclassification would take effect only from the notice date, not years back.

It gives service providers the right to petition the U.S. Tax Court for a determination of their employment status, and extends 5% withholding to the first $20,000 of compensation paid under qualifying contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Workers classified as contractors under the safe harbor would bear the full self-employment tax (both the employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare), and would not receive the employer-side payroll contributions that come with employee status. The Treasury would forgo employer-side payroll tax revenue on work shifted into the safe harbor, and workers who preferred employee status could be steered into contracts that lock in contractor treatment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Contract workers and federal payroll tax revenue

drawbacks.text: The safe harbor makes it cheap and safe for companies to keep workers out of employee status, which means no employer half of Social Security and Medicare taxes, no unemployment insurance contributions, and no pathway to employer benefits for those workers — the worker absorbs those costs instead.

The written-contract requirement is easy to satisfy (it can be signed electronically and renewed in two-year terms), so the bill could entrench contractor status across the gig economy even for workers who work in practice like employees.
The bill also raises the threshold for 1099 information reporting from $600 to $1,000 for service payments, which reduces what the IRS can cross-check against some taxpayers' returns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles real benefits: certainty for businesses, simpler tax handling and withholding for contractors, and more information reporting in some cases. But the core of the deal runs in one direction — it makes it substantially easier and safer for companies to avoid employer status, and the worker takes on the payroll taxes and benefit losses that come with that. An honest reading is that the bill's main gain accrues to contractor-dependent businesses, with the tax and benefit burden shifted onto workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Rice introduced the bill on March 7, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No representative from either party signed on as a cosponsor; the bill ended with zero cosponsors.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no committee vote, no report, no floor action — and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, since the bill did nothing; the companies that would have used the safe harbor simply kept the existing, less certain rules, while workers kept the full current-law protections against misclassification and the Treasury kept the payroll tax base.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: workers kept existing classification protections

for.name: Rep. Tom Rice
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation (Chair: Richard Neal, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a partisan split to show: its single sponsor was a Republican and it drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Gig economy platforms (ride-share, delivery, and task apps)
industries.note: The bill would give platforms a safe harbor to keep workers classified as independent contractors for tax purposes and block retroactive IRS reclassification, locking in their contractor model while adding modest withholding and reporting duties. Their gain comes largely at workers' expense, since contractors bear the full payroll tax and lose employer-side contributions and benefits.

The bill adds promotional-products sellers to the statutory nonemployee category, giving that sales channel the same tax treatment as other direct sellers. This is a narrow carve-out for a specific industry.

The bill lowers the 1099-K reporting threshold from $20,000 to $1,000 in most cases but exempts goods-focused marketplace platforms below $5,000 or 50 transactions, shifting compliance burdens unevenly across the payments industry.
